title: Non-Axisymmetric Pillar Structures due to Embedded Stars in AGN Accretion Discs
comment: 24 pages, 17 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Gravitationally unstable outer regions of AGN discs may host in situ formation of massive stars whose heating produces localized vertical "pillars" on the disc surface, in the same region that emits the broad lines. Here we investigate the reverberation-mapping signatures that such pillars would produce. We compute velocity-delay maps $Ψ(λ, τ)$, time-evolving emission-line spectra, and continuum reverberation lag spectra for these structures. We model each pillar as a 2D Gaussian perturbation to the disc height under lamp-post irradiation and weight the line response with Cloudy photoionization grids covering the major BLR lines. We show H$α$, Mg II, and C IV as representative examples. A single pillar produces a localized hotspot in $Ψ$ and a clear "S-wave" pattern in the time-evolving spectrum that persists, though diluted, for $N \sim 100$ pillars. Emission-line fluxes are suppressed in shadows behind the pillars, but when normalized by H$β$ (or by the local continuum) the line-to-H$β$ ratios move in opposite directions: Mg II/H$β$ rises while C IV/H$β$ drops. This contrast distinguishes pillars from purely kinematic features that would modulate all lines by similar factors. Across scans of the pillar shape and lamp-post height, the pillar models produce an optical continuum reverberation lag spectrum of the observed magnitude. The once-per-orbit modulation grows with $\sin i$ from foreshortening, and at sufficiently high inclination the pillar's body geometrically self-occults its lamp-facing inner slope, adding a sharper near/far contrast. These signatures provide observational diagnostics for detecting in situ star formation in AGN discs through velocity-resolved reverberation mapping campaigns.

AI.tldr: The authors model vertical "pillars" from in situ massive-star formation in AGN discs and predict their reverberation-mapping signatures—velocity-delay maps, time-evolving spectra, and continuum lag spectra—showing a characteristic "S-wave", opposed Mg II/Hβ vs C IV/Hβ responses, and inclination-dependent orbital modulation as diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Gravitationally unstable outer AGN disc regions may form massive stars in situ, whose heating creates localized vertical pillars on the disc surface within the broad-line region. No observational signature has yet been identified to detect such structures, motivating a prediction of their reverberation signatures.
AI.method: Each pillar is modeled as a 2D Gaussian perturbation to the disc height under lamp-post irradiation. The line response is weighted with Cloudy photoionization grids for major BLR lines (Hα, Mg II, C IV, Hβ). Velocity-delay maps Ψ(λ, τ), time-evolving emission-line spectra, and continuum reverberation lag spectra are computed, including scans over pillar shape and lamp-post height and inclination-dependent foreshortening and self-occultation.
AI.result: A single pillar produces a localized hotspot in Ψ and a clear "S-wave" in the time-evolving spectrum, persisting (diluted) for N~100 pillars. Line fluxes are suppressed in pillar shadows, but normalized line ratios move oppositely (Mg II/Hβ rises, C IV/Hβ drops), distinguishing pillars from purely kinematic features. The models reproduce optical continuum lag spectra of observed magnitude; once-per-orbit modulation grows with sin i, and at high inclination self-occultation sharpens near/far contrast.
AI.conclusion: These signatures offer observational diagnostics for detecting in situ star formation in AGN discs via velocity-resolved reverberation mapping campaigns, particularly through the anti-correlated Mg II/Hβ and C IV/Hβ responses and orbital modulation.

title: An Extra-nuclear Water Maser in NGC 1106 Likely Driven By An AGN Shock: Implications for Maser-based Black Hole Mass Measurements
comment: Accepted to ApJ, 11 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables
summary: We present Very Large Array A-configuration ($0.13$'') 22 GHz spectral-line and continuum observations of the Swift-BAT detected Seyfert 2 galaxy, NGC 1106, aimed at localizing a water maser line offset from the host systemic velocity by 541 km s$^{-1}$. The 22 GHz continuum emission reveals a 352 pc extended structure within the nucleus of NGC 1106, and we spatially resolve the water maser emission to a compact region $\sim1$ kpc ($3.12$'') from the nucleus. Comparing our data with previous 22 GHz 1'' observations, we found that the water maser lies near the boundary of a radio extension aligned with the jet axis, likely arising from the interface between the active galactic nucleus (AGN) outflow and the host galaxy's ISM. To verify this, we compared the water maser in NGC 1106 to a known water maser in a star-forming region within the Milky Way, along with known extragalactic water masers associated with star formation and AGN driven outflows. Overall, we found that the maser position, velocity offset, flux density, and alignment with the jet axis are consistent with an origin at the interface between the AGN outflow and the host ISM. Our results have important implications for maser-based black hole mass measurements in which disk geometry is ambiguous. Since single-dish observations cannot spatially separate disk masers from outflow-driven masers, high-velocity maser features attributed to the accretion disk may also include contributions from kpc-scale shocks.

AI.tldr: VLA A-configuration 22 GHz observations localize a 541 km/s-offset water maser ~1 kpc from the nucleus of the Seyfert 2 galaxy NGC 1106, at the boundary of a jet-aligned radio extension, indicating an origin at the AGN outflow–ISM interface rather than a circumnuclear disk.
AI.motivation: A water maser in the Swift-BAT-detected Seyfert 2 NGC 1106 is offset by 541 km/s from systemic velocity; its origin (accretion disk vs. outflow/shock) is ambiguous, and disk geometry assumptions underpin maser-based black hole mass measurements.
AI.method: VLA A-configuration 0.13'' observations at 22 GHz in spectral-line and continuum mode, spatially resolving the continuum structure and maser emission; comparison with prior 1'' 22 GHz data, and comparative analysis against a Galactic star-forming-region maser and known extragalactic star-formation and AGN-outflow masers.
AI.result: Continuum reveals a 352 pc extended nuclear structure; the maser is resolved to a compact region ~1 kpc (3.12'') from the nucleus, near the boundary of a radio extension aligned with the jet axis. Its position, velocity offset, flux density, and jet alignment are consistent with an origin at the AGN outflow–host ISM interface.
AI.conclusion: The maser is outflow/shock-driven rather than disk-associated, implying that single-dish high-velocity maser features attributed to accretion disks may include contributions from kpc-scale shocks, with important consequences for maser-based black hole mass estimates when disk geometry is ambiguous.

title: The Galactic Center Reference Frame: A 30-Year Solution
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Accepted by ApJ
summary: Stellar orbits probe the metric of and mass around the Sgr A* massive black hole. To enable study of the black hole, the surrounding mass, and tests of gravity, a precise reference frame must be established and maintained. We present an updated stellar maser-based reference frame for the inner parsec of the Galactic Center, referenced to the radio continuum of Sgr A*. This work synthesizes 30 years of astrometric observations of 15 SiO stellar masers and the Sgr A* continuum at 43 GHz. The uncertainty in the mean offset of the maser ensemble from Sgr A* is 0.08 mas in the current epoch and will decay to 0.10 mas by 2030. At a distance of 8.2 kpc, these correspond to position uncertainties of 0.6 AU and 0.8 AU, respectively, which is similar to or smaller than the stellar SiO-emitting region. The mean maser proper motion uncertainties are 0.05 mas yr$^{-1}$ in RA and 0.08 mas yr$^{-1}$ in Dec, corresponding to 1.8 km s$^{-1}$ and 3.2 km s$^{-1}$. The reference frame stability between IR and maser astrometry is 10~$μ$as yr$^{-1}$ (0.40 km s$^{-1}$) in RA and 15 $μ$as yr$^{-1}$ (0.57 km s$^{-1}$) in Dec. The masers show substantial variability in flux density and velocity structure, most notably IRS~7, which shows a 30-fold brightening in a blueshifted component since 2022. This variability may set a floor on future astrometry improvements and especially measurements of radial acceleration.

AI.tldr: A 30-year astrometric synthesis of 15 SiO stellar masers against the Sgr A* continuum yields a refined inner-parsec reference frame with sub-mas accuracy (position offsets of 0.6–0.8 AU, proper motions of 1.8–3.2 km s⁻¹), while revealing flux and velocity variability (e.g., IRS 7) that may limit future radial-acceleration measurements.
AI.motivation: Stellar orbits around Sgr A* require a precise, maintainable reference frame to probe the black hole's metric, the surrounding mass distribution, and tests of gravity. Existing frames need updating and stability quantification.
AI.method: The authors synthesized 30 years of astrometric observations of 15 SiO stellar masers together with Sgr A* continuum data at 43 GHz, constructing an updated maser-based reference frame for the inner parsec referenced to the Sgr A* radio continuum.
AI.result: Mean maser-ensemble offset from Sgr A* is 0.08 mas now, decaying to 0.10 mas by 2030 (0.6 and 0.8 AU at 8.2 kpc). Proper-motion uncertainties are 0.05 mas yr⁻¹ (RA) and 0.08 mas yr⁻¹ (Dec), i.e., 1.8 and 3.2 km s⁻¹. IR–maser frame stability is 10 μas yr⁻¹ (0.40 km s⁻¹) in RA and 15 μas yr⁻¹ (0.57 km s⁻¹) in Dec. Masers show strong flux and velocity variability, notably IRS 7 brightening 30-fold in a blueshifted component since 2022.
AI.conclusion: The maser-based frame achieves position and proper-motion precision comparable to or smaller than the stellar SiO-emitting region, supporting black hole, mass, and gravity studies. However, maser variability (especially IRS 7) may set a floor on future astrometric improvements, particularly for radial-acceleration measurements.

title: SMMAN Studies of AGN Variability. I. Long-term Spectral Evolution and a Candidate $\sim1000$-day Quasi-periodic Modulation in 4C+72.28
summary: The SMMAN project has carried out nine years of radio flux monitoring in the C and K bands of the blazar 4C+72.28. The two bands show markedly different secular evolution, with a substantially stronger K-band decline producing a gradual decrease in the C-K spectral index. After accounting for this secular evolution, multiple timing diagnostics reveal a candidate quasi-periodic modulation with a characteristic timescale of $\sim1000$ d, most clearly in the C band. The C-band GLSP peak reaches a local significance of $3.29σ$, while its global significance remains modest at $\sim2σ$ and the monitoring baseline covers only about three cycles. Independent and joint MCMC fits support a phenomenological decomposition for both bands into a long-term linear trend and a recurrent component. Under the shared-period assumption, the joint fit returns a characteristic timescale of approximately 1027 d and a similar fractional recurrent amplitudes of $\simeq5.45\%$. Information-criterion comparisons favor the combined linear-plus-sinusoidal model in both bands. Cross-correlation analysis shows a nominal K-leading offset in the original light curves but a centroid consistent with zero lag after detrending, although the lag distributions overlap substantially. These results are consistent with a common recurrent modulation superposed on slower frequency-dependent jet evolution. Geometrical Doppler-factor modulation provides one plausible interpretation, although intrinsic and opacity-related processes cannot be excluded.

AI.tldr: Nine years of C- and K-band monitoring of blazar 4C+72.28 reveal dissimilar secular trends plus a candidate ~1000 d quasi-periodic modulation, best fit by a linear trend plus sinusoid, consistent with recurrent Doppler-factor modulation on slower jet evolution.
AI.motivation: The SMMAN program aims to characterize long-term radio variability in blazar 4C+72.28 and test for quasi-periodic modulation that could probe jet physics, requiring long, multi-frequency, well-sampled light curves.
AI.method: Nine years of C- and K-band radio flux monitoring; timing diagnostics including the generalized Lomb-Scargle periodogram (GLSP) with local and global significance; independent and joint MCMC fits of a linear-trend-plus-recurrent (sinusoidal) phenomenological model; information-criterion model comparison; cross-correlation analysis before and after detrending.
AI.result: The two bands show markedly different secular evolution, with a stronger K-band decline that gradually lowers the C-K spectral index. A candidate ~1000 d modulation appears, clearest in C band (GLSP local significance 3.29σ; global ~2σ with only ~3 cycles covered). Joint fit under a shared period yields ~1027 d and fractional recurrent amplitudes of ≃5.45%. Information criteria favor the linear-plus-sinusoidal model in both bands. Cross-correlation gives a nominal K-leading offset originally but a centroid consistent with zero lag after detrending, with substantially overlapping lag distributions.
AI.conclusion: Results are consistent with a common recurrent modulation superposed on slower, frequency-dependent jet evolution; geometrical Doppler-factor modulation is a plausible interpretation, though intrinsic and opacity-related mechanisms cannot be excluded. The periodicity remains a candidate given limited cycles and modest global significance.

title: Galaxy Luminosity Functions at z~7-10 from Four Years of JWST Observations
summary: We present galaxy luminosity functions at $z\approx 7.4$ and 10 based on a comprehensive search for candidate galaxies at $6.4\lesssim z\lesssim11.3$ in JWST's public NIRCam data four years after its operation. Our work utilises nine fields covering $\sim$1,045~arcmin$^2$ in total, including seven blank fields and two galaxy cluster fields. Using the dropout technique, we selected 3,733 dropouts from the F090W passband and 2,396 dropouts from the F115W passband, which constitute the largest samples of candidate galaxies at $z\approx 7.4$ and $z\approx 10$ to date. Among these objects, 338 F090W-dropouts and 99 F115W-dropouts already have secure redshifts from JWST NIRSpec spectroscopy over four years, which we use to form two large spectroscopic subsamples to assess the magnitude-dependent contamination rates of their parent dropout samples. Our luminosity functions are based on the results after statistically correcting for both incompleteness and contamination. We find that the luminosity function at $z\approx 7.4$ can be well described by a conventional Schechter function but with a faint-end slope of $α=-1.70\pm0.16$ that is significantly shallower than most of the previous studies at $z\approx 7$--8. To verify this result, more imaging and spectroscopy at $\sim$30~mag will be needed. The luminosity function at $z\approx 10$, on the other hand, can hardly be fitted by a Schechter function but is more consistent with a power law in the form of $Φ(M)\propto 10^{-0.4(β+1)M}$, with the best-fit slope of $β=-2.36\pm0.16$. While such a behavior is largely driven by the high number densities at $M_{\rm UV}\lesssim -21.8$~mag, it is supported by the currently existing spectroscopic confirmations. Further spectroscopy at the bright end($\lesssim 26$~mag) will be needed to strengthen this result.

AI.tldr: Using JWST NIRCam data over ~1,045 arcmin² across nine fields, the authors build the largest dropout samples at z≈7.4 and z≈10 (3,733 F090W and 2,396 F115W dropouts), calibrate contamination with NIRSpec spectroscopic subsamples, and derive luminosity functions: a Schechter fit with a shallow faint-end slope α=-1.70±0.16 at z≈7.4, and a power-law fit (β=-2.36±0.16) at z≈10.
AI.motivation: Previous luminosity function measurements at z≈7–8 and z≈10 rest on small samples and uncertain contamination corrections. Large, homogeneously selected samples with spectroscopic calibration are needed to pin down the faint-end slope and the bright-end shape of the UV luminosity function in the epoch of reionization.
AI.method: Nine JWST NIRCam fields (~1,045 arcmin²; seven blank, two cluster fields). Dropout selection in F090W and F115W over 6.4≲z≲11.3. Spectroscopic subsamples of 338 F090W- and 99 F115W-dropouts with secure NIRSpec redshifts are used to measure magnitude-dependent contamination rates, which, together with incompleteness corrections, are applied statistically to the parent samples before fitting Schechter and power-law forms.
AI.result: The z≈7.4 luminosity function is well fit by a Schechter function with a faint-end slope α=-1.70±0.16, significantly shallower than most previous z≈7–8 results. The z≈10 luminosity function is poorly described by a Schechter function and is better fit by a power law, Φ(M)∝10^{-0.4(β+1)M}, with β=-2.36±0.16, driven by high number densities at M_UV≲-21.8 mag and supported by existing spectroscopic confirmations.
AI.conclusion: The largest-yet dropout samples yield a shallower faint-end slope at z≈7.4 and a power-law-like bright end at z≈10. Confirming the z≈7.4 slope requires deeper imaging and spectroscopy at ~30 mag, while strengthening the z≈10 bright-end result requires spectroscopy at ≲26 mag.

title: Differential and integral scaling laws of the mass density of molecular clouds
summary: In this work we investigate the mass density - size scaling law in molecular clouds (MCs). This relation reflects the fractal nature of MCs and plays a key role for understanding the physics, structure and evolution of these objects. We make use of the notion "ensemble of MCs", introduced in our previous work (Donkov, Veltchev \& Klessen, 2017), in which all MCs with the same probability density function (PDF) of mass density and effective size are represented by an abstract spherical cloud with the same PDF and size. In this spirit, the model is built on the base of abstract scales of the clouds' substructures (which are simply the radii of the spherical object). We consider two forms of the mass density - size scaling law: differential and integral, which in turn reveal the local and the global fractal clouds' structure. Both scaling functions are characterized by their scaling exponents, which can be explicitly expressed by the PDF of mass density, in the general case. Moreover, we derive a first order linear differential equation connecting the two scaling exponents and obtain its exact solution. As examples we apply this abstract construction to two PDFs: the so called power-law tail and the log-normal. Both have great importance for MC structure and evolution, as the latter corresponds to the earlier stages of clouds' evolution, when supersonic turbulence dominates the physical processes, while the former describes the latest stages of evolution, when star-formation takes place. The obtained results for the scaling exponents in both examples are qualitatively and numerically consistent with respective observations and simulations of MCs.

AI.tldr: The authors model the mass density–size scaling law in molecular clouds using an "ensemble" of MCs represented by an abstract spherical cloud with identical PDF and size, deriving differential and integral scaling exponents linked by a first-order linear ODE with an exact solution.
AI.motivation: The mass density–size scaling relation reflects the fractal nature of molecular clouds and is key to understanding their physics, structure, and evolution; a consistent theoretical framework connecting it to the density PDF is needed.
AI.method: Building on the "ensemble of MCs" notion (Donkov, Veltchev & Klessen 2017), each cloud is replaced by an abstract sphere sharing the same mass-density PDF and size. Two forms of the scaling law—differential (local fractal structure) and integral (global fractal structure)—are considered, with scaling exponents expressed explicitly via the mass-density PDF in the general case. A first-order linear differential equation relating the two exponents is derived and solved exactly. The construction is applied to a power-law tail PDF and a log-normal PDF.
AI.result: The two scaling exponents are explicitly expressible through the density PDF, and their connecting ODE admits an exact solution. For both the power-law-tail and log-normal PDFs, the resulting scaling exponents are qualitatively and numerically consistent with observations and simulations of MCs.
AI.conclusion: The abstract ensemble/spherical-cloud formalism provides a self-consistent analytic description of the density–size scaling law, with exponents rooted in the density PDF and matching observational and numerical results for both turbulence-dominated (log-normal) and star-forming (power-law tail) stages.

title: Binary Dynamics and Mergers in a Stellar Disk and the Formation of Dusty Objects in the Galactic Center
summary: For more than a decade, observers have been tracking a population of enigmatic dusty objects orbiting the central supermassive black hole of the Milky Way, Sagittarius A$^\star$ (SgrA$^\star$). In one interpretation, these objects are products of stellar mergers enshrouded in gaseous-dusty envelopes, which account for their infrared excess, emission lines, and stability against the tidal forces of SgrA$^\star$. Recent near-infrared observations of D9, one of the dusty objects, revealed that it embeds a spectroscopic stellar binary. In this work, we present full-fledged N-body simulations of an eccentric disk of binary stars similar to the young stellar disk observed around SgrA$^\star$. We find that some of the binaries in the disk are naturally drawn towards SgrA$^\star$ and merge there due to Kozai-Lidov (KL) oscillations in their orbits. Together with the observed nature of D9, these findings represent a self-consistent picture of how the population of the observed dusty objects could have been brought into existence. The binary fraction in our N-body model evolves to increase with distance from SgrA$^\star$, which is also in agreement with the observational constraints. Our simulations also suggest that beside the dusty objects, stellar mergers are present within the young stellar disk, which could be identified as chemically peculiar or fast-rotating stars. Our results show that dynamical evolution of binary stars in the young stellar disk plays a crucial role in shaping the stellar content in the Galactic Center.

AI.tldr: N-body simulations of an eccentric disk of binary stars around SgrA* show that Kozai-Lidov oscillations drive some binaries inward to merge near the black hole, naturally explaining the population of dusty objects (including the binary-embedding D9) and predicting a binary fraction increasing with distance.
AI.motivation: The origin of the enigmatic dusty objects orbiting SgrA* is debated; one hypothesis is that they are merged stellar binaries enshrouded in gaseous-dusty envelopes, and the recent detection of a spectroscopic stellar binary inside D9 motivates testing whether a young binary-star disk can dynamically deliver mergers to the Galactic Center.
AI.method: Full N-body simulations of an eccentric disk of binary stars modeled after the observed young stellar disk around SgrA*, tracking dynamical evolution including Kozai-Lidov oscillations of binary orbits.
AI.result: Some binaries are driven toward SgrA* and merge there via Kozai-Lidov oscillations; the binary fraction in the model evolves to increase with galactocentric distance, matching observational constraints; mergers are predicted within the young stellar disk, identifiable as chemically peculiar or fast-rotating stars.
AI.conclusion: Dynamical evolution of binary stars in the young stellar disk, combined with the observed nature of D9, provides a self-consistent scenario for forming the dusty objects and plays a key role in shaping the stellar content of the Galactic Center.

title: From Inspiral to Outburst: Modeling a Potential Luminous Red Nova from Betelgeuse
summary: Recent evidence suggests that Betelgeuse may host a stellar companion whose orbit will decay through tidal interactions, ultimately leading to engulfment and merger within the next several thousand years. If confirmed, this system could represent the nearest and best-characterized progenitor of a future luminous red nova (LRN). We investigate whether the shock-breakout and cooling emission preceding the LRN can be used to constrain the properties of the companion and its disruption within the stellar envelope. Using binary stellar evolution calculations, we evolve Betelgeuse with companions of $0.7$, $1.0$, and $2.0 M_\odot$ to the onset of common envelope evolution (CEE). We then perform one-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamic simulations that follow companion disruption, energy deposition, and shock propagation through the envelope. We find that the peak luminosity increases systematically with companion mass, from $2.44\times10^{41}$ to $6.17\times10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$ across the $0.7$-$2.0 M_\odot$ models, while the duration increases more modestly from $1.48$ to $1.99$ days and attains apparent magnitudes brighter than Venus as viewed from Earth. Tidal disruption contributes both kinetic energy and mass to the envelope, linking the companion's structure and mass to the energetics of the shock-heated ejecta. The monotonic luminosity sequence demonstrates that the early breakout emission can retain direct information about the engulfed companion. The interaction ejects $6.15$-$11.19 M_\odot$ of hydrogen-rich material, substantially modifying both the envelope structure and circumstellar environment prior to core collapse.

AI.tldr: Betelgeuse may host a companion that will merge within thousands of years, making it the nearest progenitor of a luminous red nova (LRN). Using binary evolution plus 1D radiation-hydrodynamic simulations for companions of 0.7, 1.0, and 2.0 M_sun, we show that pre-LRN shock-breakout emission scales monotonically with companion mass and thus encodes the companion's properties.
AI.motivation: Betelgeuse is suspected to host a stellar companion whose orbit decays tidally toward engulfment and merger within several thousand years, potentially making it the nearest, best-characterized future LRN progenitor. The authors ask whether shock-breakout and cooling emission preceding the LRN can constrain the companion's properties and its disruption within the envelope.
AI.method: Binary stellar evolution calculations evolve Betelgeuse with 0.7, 1.0, and 2.0 M_sun companions to the onset of common envelope evolution (CEE). One-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamic simulations then follow companion disruption, energy deposition, and shock propagation through the envelope.
AI.result: Peak luminosity rises systematically with companion mass, from 2.44e41 to 6.17e41 erg/s across 0.7-2.0 M_sun, while duration increases modestly from 1.48 to 1.99 days; events reach apparent magnitudes brighter than Venus as seen from Earth. Tidal disruption supplies both kinetic energy and mass to the envelope, linking companion structure and mass to the energetics of shock-heated ejecta. The interaction ejects 6.15-11.19 M_sun of hydrogen-rich material.
AI.conclusion: The monotonic luminosity sequence shows early breakout emission retains direct information about the engulfed companion, offering a diagnostic of companion mass. The merger ejecta substantially modify both the envelope structure and the circumstellar environment prior to core collapse.

title: Local Analogs of Little Red Dots: Clues to the X-ray Weakness
comment: Accepted. Our custom EP-FXT data analysis software available at https://github.com/AstroChensj/eFXTDAS. Comments are welcome!
summary: A major question about JWST's little red dots (LRDs) at $z\sim4-8$ is the origin of their apparent X-ray weakness. Even deep Chandra stacks yield only tentative detections or broad-band limits and cannot distinguish among super-Eddington accretion, intrinsic X-ray weakness, and Compton-thick (CT) obscuration. Local analogs offer a powerful complementary route. At $z\sim0.3$, similarly luminous sources require $\sim10^{3-4}$ less exposure for comparable signal-to-noise, suffer less source confusion, and directly probe the diagnostic rest-frame soft X-rays. Here we present a pilot Einstein Probe/FXT study of six "local little red dots" (LLRDs), V-shaped broad-line green pea galaxies selected as low-redshift counterparts of LRDs. These sources show X-ray diversity: "X-normal" LLRDs resemble type 1 AGNs in X-ray luminosity and optical variability, whereas the "X-weak" stack lies $\sim0.5-0.7$ dex below standard unobscured-quasar scaling relations while remaining compatible with the representative LRD stack and 95% of published individual limits. The X-weak LLRDs also lack detected optical variability and have redder optical continua than X-normal LLRDs, making their V-shaped SEDs closer to those of high-redshift LRDs. The detection of the X-weak stack at $\sim3.3σ$ with the soft-X-ray-sensitive EP-FXT provides rest-frame $\sim2-3$ keV constraints difficult to reconcile with a typical unobscured super-Eddington model or a local-AGN-like CT geometry examined here, although modified variants remain possible. The simplest alternative is a mildly X-ray-weak corona ($Δα_{\mathrm{ox}}\sim-0.1$ to $-0.2$) with Compton-thin absorption ($N_{\mathrm{H}}\sim10^{22-23}$ cm$^{-2}$), consistent with the independent Balmer decrement/break diagnostics. Together with growing samples of local LRD analogs, our results offer a practical path for testing the physical nature of LRD X-ray weakness.

AI.tldr: A pilot Einstein Probe/FXT study of six local little red dots (LLRDs)—V-shaped broad-line green peas at z~0.3—reveals X-ray diversity (X-normal vs. X-weak), and the X-weak stack (detected at ~3.3σ) favors a mildly X-ray-weak corona with Compton-thin absorption over unobscured super-Eddington or Compton-thick scenarios.
AI.motivation: JWST's little red dots at z~4–8 appear X-ray weak, but even deep Chandra stacks give only tentative detections or broad-band limits that cannot disentangle super-Eddington accretion, intrinsic X-ray weakness, and Compton-thick obscuration. Local analogs provide a complementary route: at z~0.3, comparably luminous sources need ~10^{3–4} less exposure, suffer less source confusion, and directly probe rest-frame soft X-rays.
AI.method: Pilot Einstein Probe/FXT observations of six "local little red dots" (LLRDs)—V-shaped broad-line green pea galaxies at z~0.3 selected as low-redshift LRD counterparts. The authors compare their X-ray luminosities, optical variability, and optical colors, stacking the X-weak sub-sample and comparing against unobscured-quasar scaling relations, the representative LRD stack, published individual limits, and independent Balmer decrement/break diagnostics.
AI.result: The LLRDs show X-ray diversity: X-normal sources resemble type 1 AGNs in X-ray luminosity and optical variability, while the X-weak stack lies ~0.5–0.7 dex below standard unobscured-quasar scaling relations, consistent with the LRD stack and 95% of published individual limits. X-weak LLRDs lack detected optical variability and have redder continua, making their V-shaped SEDs closer to high-z LRDs. The X-weak stack is detected at ~3.3σ, giving rest-frame ~2–3 keV constraints hard to reconcile with a typical unobscured super-Eddington model or a local-AGN-like Compton-thick geometry, though modified variants remain possible.
AI.conclusion: The simplest explanation is a mildly X-ray-weak corona (Δα_ox ~ -0.1 to -0.2) with Compton-thin absorption (N_H ~ 10^{22–23} cm^{-2}), consistent with independent Balmer decrement/break diagnostics. Together with growing samples of local LRD analogs, local studies offer a practical path to test the physical nature of LRD X-ray weakness.

title: FastSpec: Fast and versatile stellar spectrum synthesis code
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures: Astronomy & Astrophysics, in press
summary: Modelling data from modern spectroscopic surveys and time-resolved spectropolarimetric observations requires stellar synthetic spectra to be computed rapidly over wide wavelength ranges from line lists that increasingly reach hundreds of millions of transitions. Spectropolarimetric analyses of magnetically active stars additionally demand a solution of the polarised radiative transfer problem. We present FastSpec, a new LTE spectrum synthesis code designed around two goals: increased raw computational speed and broad astrophysical applicability, including the calculation of the full Stokes vector in the presence of a magnetic field. FastSpec computes emergent intensity and flux spectra from plane-parallel and spherical model atmospheres. Chemical and ionisation equilibrium is obtained from the updated SME equation-of-state package, continuum opacities follow the ATLAS family of routines, hydrogen bound-bound and bound-free absorption uses the occupation-probability formalism, and line absorption is evaluated with fast table-based Voigt and Faraday-Voigt profile algorithms. The transfer equation is integrated with DELO-Bezier formal solvers in both scalar and Stokes-vector form. Speed is achieved through aggressive OpenMP parallelisation, adaptive per-line wavelength windowing, and a memory-capped block-processing scheme that lets arbitrarily large line lists be handled within a user-defined RAM budget. The code synthesises spectra thousands of Å wide from line lists of $10^8$ molecular and atomic transitions in under a minute on a modern multi-core laptop while reproducing benchmark calculations from established codes. FastSpec combines the physical completeness of classical model atmosphere and spectrum synthesis codes with the speed required by large surveys and the polarised transfer needed for stellar magnetism studies into a single portable package.

AI.tldr: FastSpec is a new LTE spectrum synthesis code that computes wide-wavelength stellar spectra (including full Stokes vector polarised transfer) rapidly from line lists with ~10^8 transitions in under a minute on a multicore laptop, while reproducing established benchmark calculations.
AI.motivation: Modern spectroscopic surveys and time-resolved spectropolarimetry require stellar synthetic spectra computed rapidly over wide wavelength ranges from line lists reaching hundreds of millions of transitions. Spectropolarimetric analyses of magnetically active stars additionally demand solving the polarised radiative transfer problem, which existing tools address slowly or incompletely.
AI.method: FastSpec computes emergent intensity and flux spectra from plane-parallel and spherical model atmospheres. It uses the updated SME equation-of-state package for chemical/ionisation equilibrium, ATLAS-family continuum opacities, occupation-probability formalism for hydrogen bound-bound and bound-free absorption, and fast table-based Voigt and Faraday-Voigt profiles for line absorption. The transfer equation is integrated with DELO-Bezier formal solvers in scalar and Stokes-vector form. Speed comes from aggressive OpenMP parallelisation, adaptive per-line wavelength windowing, and a memory-capped block-processing scheme handling arbitrarily large line lists within a user-defined RAM budget.
AI.result: The code synthesises spectra thousands of Ångströms wide from line lists of 10^8 molecular and atomic transitions in under a minute on a modern multi-core laptop, while reproducing benchmark calculations from established codes.
AI.conclusion: FastSpec combines the physical completeness of classical model-atmosphere and spectrum-synthesis codes with the speed required by large surveys and the polarised transfer needed for stellar magnetism studies, all in a single portable package.

title: Star clusters at cosmic dawn I: the emergence of the initial cluster mass function
summary: JWST observations of lensed galaxies reveal unusually bright star-cluster candidates within the first billion years after the Big Bang. However, the physical processes shaping the initial cluster mass function (ICMF) remain uncertain. We study the formation of a galaxy embedded in a dark matter halo whose virial mass reaches $10^{10} \mathrm{M}_\odot$ at $z=6$, using cosmological radiation-hydrodynamics zoom-in simulations. Its star clusters, represented by sink particles, accrete gas and form stellar populations that supply radiation and supernova feedback, thereby regulating their own growth. As we do not prescribe an efficiency per free-fall time or a fixed star-cluster formation duration, the ICMF emerges self-consistently. We assess the effects of numerical resolution and stellar radiation. Schechter fits to the central-galaxy ICMF give truncation masses near $6 \times 10^6 \mathrm{M}_\odot$, with substantial uncertainty. At fixed resolution, including stellar radiation makes the low-mass slope of the ICMF shallower, from $-1.60$ to $-1.34$, while doubling the spatial resolution steepens it back to $-1.54$. Stellar radiation also reduces the abundance of low-mass clouds, particularly those with lower gas densities, and shortens the formation time of star clusters to about a Myr, i.e. well before their first supernovae go off. On average, more rapidly fed star clusters accrete for longer, making their final masses rise faster than linearly with the initial accretion rate and contributing to a flatter ICMF. At fixed host-galaxy star formation rate, our brightest simulated clusters reach UV luminosities comparable to those of observed lensed star-cluster candidates.

AI.tldr: Cosmological radiation-hydrodynamics zoom-in simulations of a z=6 galaxy show that the initial cluster mass function emerges self-consistently, with stellar radiation flattening its low-mass slope and rapid gas accretion producing brighter, longer-accreting clusters.
AI.motivation: JWST has revealed unusually bright star-cluster candidates in galaxies within the first billion years, but the physical processes setting the initial cluster mass function (ICMF) are uncertain.
AI.method: Radiation-hydrodynamics zoom-in simulations of a galaxy in a dark matter halo reaching 10^10 Msun at z=6. Star clusters are modeled as accreting sink particles that feed back via radiation and supernovae and regulate their own growth, with no prescribed star-formation efficiency or cluster formation duration. The authors test numerical resolution and stellar radiation effects and fit Schechter functions to the central-galaxy ICMF.
AI.result: Schechter truncation masses are ~6x10^6 Msun with large uncertainty. At fixed resolution, stellar radiation shallows the low-mass slope from -1.60 to -1.34; doubling spatial resolution steepens it to -1.54. Radiation reduces low-mass, low-density clouds and shortens cluster formation times to ~1 Myr, before the first supernovae. Faster-fed clusters accrete longer, so final mass rises faster than linearly with initial accretion rate, flattening the ICMF. Brightest simulated clusters reach UV luminosities comparable to observed lensed candidates at fixed host SFR.
AI.conclusion: The ICMF can emerge self-consistently from accretion and feedback physics; stellar radiation and resolution significantly shape its slope, and the resulting bright clusters can reproduce JWST-observed lensed star-cluster candidates.

title: Probing Red Giant Interiors with g-Dominated Mixed Modes II: The Cases of KIC 6117517, KIC 9475697, KIC 10123207 and KIC 10200377
comment: 28 pages, 15 figures, 14 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Building on Paper~I, which constrained core overshooting to $f_{\rm ov} < 0.01$ for $M < 1.4\,M_{\odot}$ and found $α_{\rm MLT} \simeq 2.0$ for metal-rich red giants, we extend this analysis to four lower-mass \textit{Kepler} red giants spanning a broad metallicity range: KIC~6117517, KIC~9475697, KIC~10123207, and KIC~10200377. Two complementary model grids are constructed: Grid~A fixes $α_{\rm MLT} = 2.0$ while varying metallicity; Grid~B adopts spectroscopic metallicities with $α_{\rm MLT}$ as a free parameter. Grid~A successfully reproduces both asteroseismic and spectroscopic constraints for the metal-rich targets (KIC~6117517 and KIC~9475697), confirming $α_{\rm MLT} = 2.0$ for metal-rich red giants. For the metal-poor targets (KIC~10123207 and KIC~10200377), Grid~B yields larger mixing-length parameters of $α_{\rm MLT} \approx 2.16$--$2.18$. Although only four stars are analyzed with unequal sensitivity to $α_{\rm MLT}$, these results suggest a tentative increase in convective efficiency toward lower metallicity, consistent with 3D hydrodynamical simulations but opposite to some 1D empirical calibrations. The best-fitting overshooting parameters ($f_{\rm ov} = 0.006$--$0.007$) independently support the Paper~I constraint and are consistent with a mass-dependent overshooting relation. The parameter uncertainties reach $0.6$--$2.5\%$ in mass, $0.2$--$0.9\%$ in radius, $2$--$13\%$ in age, and below $0.6\%$ in helium-core mass and below $0.2\%$ in helium-core radius. Surface-effect corrections are negligible for g-dominated mixed modes, validating $χ^2_{l=1g}$ as a robust fitting metric. For KIC~9475697, the core rotation rate is determined to be $Ω_{\rm core} = 0.6945 \pm 0.0190\,μ$Hz from model-based trapping parameters.

AI.tldr: Extending Paper I to four lower-mass Kepler red giants, the study finds α_MLT ≈ 2.0 for metal-rich stars and a tentative increase to α_MLT ≈ 2.16–2.18 for metal-poor stars, with overshooting f_ov = 0.006–0.007 supporting the earlier constraint and tight asteroseismic parameter uncertainties.
AI.motivation: Paper I constrained core overshooting (f_ov < 0.01) for M < 1.4 M_sun and found α_MLT ≈ 2.0 for metal-rich red giants. This work tests whether that mixing-length calibration holds across a broader metallicity range in lower-mass red giants, addressing the metallicity dependence of convective efficiency and providing independent checks on overshooting.
AI.method: Analyzes four low-mass Kepler red giants (KIC 6117517, 9475697, 10123207, 10200377) spanning a wide metallicity range using two grids: Grid A fixes α_MLT = 2.0 while varying metallicity; Grid B uses spectroscopic metallicities with α_MLT free. Models are constrained by asteroseismic (χ²_{l=1g}) and spectroscopic data; core rotation is inferred from model-based mixed-mode trapping parameters.
AI.result: Grid A reproduces both asteroseismic and spectroscopic constraints for the metal-rich targets (KIC 6117517, 9475697), confirming α_MLT = 2.0. For the metal-poor targets (KIC 10123207, 10200377), Grid B gives α_MLT ≈ 2.16–2.18. Best-fit f_ov = 0.006–0.007 independently supports the Paper I constraint and a mass-dependent overshooting relation. Uncertainties: 0.6–2.5% in mass, 0.2–0.9% in radius, 2–13% in age, <0.6% in He-core mass, <0.2% in He-core radius. Surface-effect corrections are negligible for g-dominated mixed modes. For KIC 9475697, Ω_core = 0.6945 ± 0.0190 μHz.
AI.conclusion: Results suggest a tentative increase in convective efficiency toward lower metallicity, consistent with 3D hydrodynamical simulations but opposite to some 1D empirical calibrations. The overshooting values reinforce Paper I and a mass-dependent overshooting relation. The findings are limited by the small sample (four stars) and unequal sensitivity to α_MLT, so the metallicity trend remains tentative; χ²_{l=1g} is validated as a robust fitting metric for g-dominated mixed modes.

title: The Galactic rotation curve from the ALS III catalogue of OB Stars
summary: The Galactic rotation curve reveals the radial mass distribution of the Milky Way, but its determination depends on the tracer population. Young massive stars are the least dynamically evolved tracer, retaining the kinematics of the gas from which they formed, yet previous determinations from OB stars were confined to the solar neighbourhood. We determine the rotation curve and the solar motion from 14017 spectroscopically confirmed OB stars from the ALS III catalogue, using Gaia DR3 five-dimensional astrometry with revised distances and corrected proper motions. The curve is parameterised as a fourth-degree Chebyshev polynomial in Galactocentric radius and fitted to the proper motions by weighted least squares, solving simultaneously for the solar motion. Uncertainties are derived from 1000 bootstrap resamplings. We obtain a circular velocity at the solar radius (8.178 kpc) of 236.3 +/- 1.1 km/s, solar motion components U = 8.06 +/- 0.41, V = 10.91 +/- 0.86 and W = 7.53 +/- 0.14 km/s, and Oort constants A = 16.35 +/- 0.21 and B = -12.54 +/- 0.19 km/s/kpc. The curve rises inside the solar circle and declines gently beyond it, with a local gradient of -3.81 +/- 0.38 km/s/kpc, and is constrained between 5.5 and 11 kpc. Because the tracer is dynamically cold and the proper motions are fitted directly, no asymmetric drift correction or Jeans modelling is required, so the systematics differ from those affecting older tracers. The gentle decline beyond the solar radius agrees with determinations from older tracers where they overlap, making it unlikely to be a methodological artefact. Only the solar radial motion is poorly constrained by tangential data, without affecting the curve. The stars departing most from the curve (1474 to 1662, depending on the selection criterion) form the largest sample of OB runaway candidates to date, to be analysed in a forthcoming paper based on Gaia DR4.

AI.tldr: Determination of the Milky Way rotation curve and solar motion from 14,017 spectroscopically confirmed OB stars using Gaia DR3 5D astrometry, yielding V(R0)=236.3 km/s, solar motion (U,V,W)=(8.06,10.91,7.53) km/s, and Oort constants A=16.35, B=-12.54 km/s/kpc, with the curve rising inside and gently declining beyond the solar circle (local gradient -3.81 km/s/kpc) constrained between 5.5 and 11 kpc.
AI.motivation: The Galactic rotation curve traces the radial mass distribution of the Milky Way but its determination is tracer-dependent. Young massive OB stars are the least dynamically evolved tracer, preserving the kinematics of their birth gas, yet prior OB-based determinations were restricted to the solar neighbourhood. This work extends the analysis to a much larger, spatially extended sample.
AI.method: Uses 14,017 spectroscopically confirmed OB stars from the ALS III catalogue with Gaia DR3 five-dimensional astrometry, revised distances, and corrected proper motions. The rotation curve is parameterised as a fourth-degree Chebyshev polynomial in Galactocentric radius and fitted to proper motions via weighted least squares, solving simultaneously for the solar motion. Uncertainties come from 1000 bootstrap resamplings. No asymmetric drift correction or Jeans modelling is needed because the tracer is dynamically cold and proper motions are fitted directly.
AI.result: Circular velocity at the solar radius (8.178 kpc) of 236.3 ± 1.1 km/s; solar motion U = 8.06 ± 0.41, V = 10.91 ± 0.86, W = 7.53 ± 0.14 km/s; Oort constants A = 16.35 ± 0.21 and B = -12.54 ± 0.19 km/s/kpc. The curve rises inside the solar circle and declines gently beyond it with local gradient -3.81 ± 0.38 km/s/kpc, constrained between 5.5 and 11 kpc. Outliers (1474–1662 depending on selection) form the largest OB runaway candidate sample to date.
AI.conclusion: The gentle decline beyond the solar radius agrees with determinations from older tracers where they overlap, making a methodological artefact unlikely. The systematics differ from older tracers due to the dynamically cold tracer and direct proper-motion fitting. Only the solar radial motion is poorly constrained by tangential data, without affecting the curve. The runaway candidates will be analysed in a forthcoming paper based on Gaia DR4.

title: A comprehensive reanalysis of HD 99458. Not a magnetic Ap star but an oscillating Algol with ongoing mass transfer
comment: 34 pages, 31 figures, 18 tables (including the full Table A.1.), 3 appendices. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Context. Since 2019, HD 99458 has been known as a unique example of a $δ$ Sct variable with chemical peculiarities of Ap type in an eclipsing binary. Aims. We aim to review the peculiar status of the star with new observational materials. Methods. The current study is the result of meticulous analysis of space-based photometry from Kepler K2 and TESS, multi-site spectroscopic and spectropolarimetric observations, as well as speckle-interferometric data. Asteroseismic modelling of stellar pulsation is an essential part of the research. Results. We find HD 99458 to be an eclipsing Algol-type system with active mass transfer from the cool companion filling its Roche lobe to the pulsating primary. We identified signatures of a disc and accretion with varying rates in spectra and light curves. The system's orbital period increases with the rate $\dot{P}_\mathrm{orb}$ of 5.045 s yr$^{-1}$, indicating potential multiplicity. We failed to detect traces of the primary's magnetic field or excessive abundances, both of which are necessary to classify HD 99458 as an Ap star. We have constrained the fundamental parameters of the pulsating primary and analysed its pulsation using asteroseismology. In space-based photometry, we identified pulsation modes with angular degree $\ell\leq3$. Two-dimensional Fourier analysis of spectroscopic time series reveals pulsations in the form of standing waves with the azimuthal orders $|m|=5\pm1$. Combined analysis of photometry and spectroscopy confirms the status of HD 99458 as a triaxial gravitationally distorted pulsator. Conclusions. Our comprehensive study affirms the new classification for HD 99458.

AI.tldr: HD 99458 is reclassified from an Ap-type δ Sct in an eclipsing binary to an Algol-type eclipsing system undergoing active mass transfer onto a pulsating primary, with no detectable magnetic field or chemical peculiarities.
AI.motivation: Since 2019 HD 99458 has been regarded as a unique example of a δ Sct variable with Ap chemical peculiarities in an eclipsing binary; the authors aim to reassess this peculiar status using new observational material.
AI.method: Analysis of Kepler K2 and TESS space photometry, multi-site spectroscopy and spectropolarimetry, speckle interferometry, and asteroseismic modelling of the pulsations (including 2D Fourier analysis of spectroscopic time series).
AI.result: The system is an eclipsing Algol-type binary with the cool companion filling its Roche lobe and transferring mass to the pulsating primary; disc and variable accretion signatures appear in spectra and light curves; the orbital period increases at a rate of 5.045 s yr⁻¹, suggesting additional multiplicity. No magnetic field or abundance anomalies are detected. Pulsation modes with ℓ ≤ 3 are identified in photometry, while spectroscopy reveals standing waves with |m| = 5 ± 1, confirming a triaxial, gravitationally distorted pulsator.
AI.conclusion: The comprehensive study supports a revised classification of HD 99458, removing its status as an Ap star and establishing it as a mass-transferring Algol binary hosting a tidally distorted pulsator.

title: Forward model of the Gaia DR3 selection function
summary: The completeness of an astronomical catalogue depends on its selection function, which is a combination of the observing strategy, instrumental characteristics, and intrinsic properties of the sources being observed. This is particularly complex for Gaia, whose non-uniform scanning law and onboard prioritisation of bright sources in dense areas make its selection function vary strongly with celestial position and source brightness. We estimate the Gaia DR3 source catalogue selection function across the whole sky and over the full magnitude range, using only data from the Gaia catalogue and knowledge of the nominal scanning law as provided by the Gaia Observation Forecast Tool. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian model that estimates the number of times Gaia scanned each celestial position jointly with the source detection efficiency, and fit it via Markov chain Monte Carlo to the 1 806 196 447 sources in Gaia DR3 with reported celestial positions, G magnitudes, and astrometric matched transit counts. Gaia DR3 is essentially complete for G in (5, 19.5) in the on-sky median. After that, the completeness decreases with magnitude according to the scanning law pattern combined with the imprint of crowded regions. The completeness is also lower at the very bright end of the survey, consistent with the known limitations on Gaia observations of bright stars. We find an unexpected completeness increase beyond G ~ 21, which we conclude is an artefact caused by extended sources, as confirmed by cross-matching against Euclid's Q1 catalogue. Treating the scanning law as part of the inference process, and anchoring it to all Gaia DR3 sources of all magnitudes on a fine-grained grid on the sky, removes the need for an explicit crowding correction. The resulting selection function, valid everywhere where Gaia data are available, is released as part of the GaiaUnlimited Python package. [abridged]

AI.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model estimates the Gaia DR3 catalogue selection function across the whole sky and full magnitude range by jointly inferring scanning-law transit counts and detection efficiency from 1.8 billion sources, without needing an explicit crowding correction.
AI.motivation: Gaia's selection function is complex due to its non-uniform scanning law and onboard prioritisation of bright sources in dense areas, making completeness vary strongly with sky position and brightness; an accurate, spatially resolved selection function is needed for catalogue completeness.
AI.method: A hierarchical Bayesian model jointly estimates the number of Gaia scans per celestial position and the source detection efficiency, fitted via MCMC to the 1,806,196,447 Gaia DR3 sources with positions, G magnitudes, and astrometric matched transit counts, using the nominal scanning law from the Gaia Observation Forecast Tool; the scanning law is treated as part of the inference on a fine sky grid.
AI.result: Gaia DR3 is essentially complete for G in (5, 19.5) in the on-sky median; completeness then declines with magnitude per the scanning-law pattern plus crowding imprint, is lower at the bright end, and shows an unexpected increase beyond G~21 found to be an artefact from extended sources (confirmed via cross-match with Euclid Q1).
AI.conclusion: Anchoring the scanning law to all Gaia DR3 sources removes the need for explicit crowding correction, yielding a selection function valid wherever Gaia data exist, released as part of the GaiaUnlimited Python package.

title: Accuracy of electric current inference assuming three-dimensional hydrostatic equilibrium
summary: The chromospheric and coronal heating problem is among the major open questions in solar physics. Some of the possible mechanisms that can explain the rise in temperature that is needed to reproduce the observations require the estimation of electric currents. Since these depend on the spatial derivatives of the magnetic field components, it is necessary to obtain the full magnetic field vector from observational data in a 3D geometrical grid. We developed a new method to obtain the 3D geometrical configuration of the atmosphere using the approximation of hydrostatic equilibrium in three dimensions to determine the gas pressure and density as a function of optical depth, column mass, or geometrical distance. This development has been designed as an extension for any inversion code that outputs a stratification of temperature and gas pressure or density to enable the estimation of electric current densities from observations. We investigated our approach using a snapshot from a sunspot MHD simulation. The difference between the solver output and the simulation, taken as the ground truth, is mostly between 30 and 45 %, showing a similar pattern over a large optical depth range. Additional tests also showed that the solver provides a unique solution, has a scarce sensitivity to the boundary condition and is only marginally impacted by the viewing angle. We conclude that the electric currents can be inferred at a reasonable accuracy with this approach using the simulation parameters as input. We also tested set-ups that aim at mimicking more realistic cases, where the code performed equally well. The results in this work show promise with respect to future applications to spectropolarimetric data, however, some additional challenges will need to be adressed when moving from the controlled input of the simulation to observational data.

AI.tldr: The authors present a new method to reconstruct the 3D geometrical configuration of the solar atmosphere under the approximation of hydrostatic equilibrium, enabling estimation of electric current densities from observational data as an extension to existing inversion codes.
AI.motivation: The chromospheric and coronal heating problem requires estimation of electric currents, which depend on spatial derivatives of magnetic field components. Obtaining the full magnetic field vector in a 3D geometrical grid from observational data necessitates a method to determine the 3D atmosphere configuration.
AI.method: The method approximates hydrostatic equilibrium in three dimensions to determine gas pressure and density as a function of optical depth, column mass, or geometrical distance. It is designed as an extension for any inversion code that outputs stratification of temperature and gas pressure or density, enabling estimation of electric current densities. The approach was tested on a snapshot from a sunspot MHD simulation against ground truth.
AI.result: The difference between solver output and simulation ground truth is mostly between 30 and 45%, with a similar pattern over a large optical depth range. Additional tests showed the solver provides a unique solution, has scarce sensitivity to the boundary condition, and is only marginally affected by viewing angle. Setups mimicking more realistic cases performed equally well.
AI.conclusion: Electric currents can be inferred at reasonable accuracy with this approach using simulation parameters as input. The results are promising for future applications to spectropolarimetric data, though additional challenges must be addressed when moving from controlled simulation input to observational data.

title: Polarization Observations of NGC 315 with FAST
summary: We present new continuum and polarization observations of radio galaxy NGC 315 obtained with the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) over 1.0-1.5 GHz. The FAST data detect diffuse large-scale polarized emission with a noise level of 0.065 mJy beam$^{-1}$ at resolution of $4'$. We derived a rotation measure (RM) map with an error of 1.1 rad m$^{-2}$ including systematic error. The intrinsic RM map was obtained after subtracting the Galactic foreground contribution. We estimated a total magnetic field strength of $\lesssim 1$ $μ$G across the source and a thermal electron density of $\sim 10^{-4}$ cm$^{-3}$ toward the northwest lobe. The fractional polarization analysis suggests a random magnetic-field component over a large area toward the northwest lobe.

AI.tldr: FAST observations of NGC 315 at 1.0–1.5 GHz reveal diffuse large-scale polarized emission and an intrinsic rotation measure map, yielding a total magnetic field ≲1 μG and random field components in the northwest lobe.
AI.motivation: Obtain high-sensitivity, low-frequency continuum and polarization data to characterize the diffuse polarized emission, rotation measure, and magnetic field properties of radio galaxy NGC 315, which are difficult to access with prior instruments.
AI.method: Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) continuum and polarization observations over 1.0–1.5 GHz at 4′ resolution; rotation measure (RM) mapping with foreground correction and fractional polarization analysis.
AI.result: Noise level of 0.065 mJy beam⁻¹; RM map with 1.1 rad m⁻² error (including systematic); total magnetic field strength ≲1 μG across the source; thermal electron density ~10⁻⁴ cm⁻³ toward the northwest lobe; evidence for a random magnetic-field component over a large area in the northwest lobe.
AI.conclusion: FAST enables detection of diffuse large-scale polarized emission in NGC 315, and the derived RM and field estimates indicate weak total fields with substantial random components in the northwest lobe.

title: ARENA: Active Region attENtion Aggregation for interpretable solar flare prediction
comment: 7+12 pages (2+8 figures), accepted at the "Representations for the Physical Sciences" workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Predicting solar flares is a challenging space-weather forecasting problem with potentially significant impacts on Earth's upper atmosphere, including disruptions to radio communications. We propose Active Region attENtion Aggregation (ARENA), a neural network architecture that predicts solar flares from a variable number of active-region cutouts while learning to identify the region most relevant to the prediction. ARENA is trained using multiple-instance learning under weak supervision, requiring only a flare/no-flare label for the observation and no labels specifying the flare origin. The learned attention mechanism therefore provides a means of localizing the active region driving the prediction without explicit origin annotations. ARENA achieves a heidke skill score of 0.45 which is comparable to other flare prediction approaches. These results demonstrate that active-region-based aggregation can provide an efficient and interpretable approach to solar flare prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/LuisBauer22/ARENA.

AI.tldr: ARENA is an attention-based neural network that predicts solar flares from sets of active-region cutouts using multiple-instance learning under weak supervision, achieving a Heidke skill score of 0.45 while localizing the responsible region without origin labels.
AI.motivation: Solar flare prediction is a challenging space-weather problem with significant impacts on Earth's upper atmosphere, including radio communication disruptions. Existing approaches typically require explicit flare-origin annotations, which are costly to obtain.
AI.method: ARENA (Active Region attENtion Aggregation) aggregates a variable number of active-region cutouts via a learned attention mechanism. It is trained with multiple-instance learning under weak supervision, using only a flare/no-flare label for the full observation, and no labels specifying the flare origin.
AI.result: ARENA achieves a Heidke skill score of 0.45, comparable to other flare prediction approaches. The learned attention mechanism additionally localizes the active region driving the prediction, providing interpretability without explicit origin annotations.
AI.conclusion: Active-region-based aggregation offers an efficient and interpretable approach to solar flare prediction. Code is publicly available.

title: Spatial distribution of star formation in dwarf galaxies: Merger-driven and secular starburst
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A, 8 pages, 4 figures
summary: Galaxy interactions can induce bursts of star formation (SF), while internal or secular processes can also trigger starbursts (SB). Recent studies of the spatial distribution of SF in high-mass (M$_{*}>10^{10}M_{\odot}$) SB galaxies show that SF is centrally concentrated in merger-driven SBs, whereas in secularly driven SB systems, SF is uniformly enhanced across the system. However, it is not clear whether such distinct spatial signatures are present in low-mass (M$_{*} < 10^{10} M_{\odot}$) SB galaxies. In this context, we studied the SF properties of a sample of 272 isolated SB (i.e., with no massive galaxy, within a 1 Mpc$^3$ volume) dwarf galaxies consisting of 17 post-merger and 255 non-interacting SB galaxies, spanning a stellar mass range of $10^{7}-10^{9.6} M_{\odot}$ and a redshift range of 0.01-0.12. For this study, we utilise FUV imaging data from GALEX to estimate the star formation rates of our sample galaxies. We investigated the spatial variation of SB activity by comparing star formation rate surface density (SFRD) across radial bins for post-merger and non-interacting samples of dwarfs. We find an enhancement in SFRD across all radial bins for both samples, and that the enhancement is more or less uniform across the galaxy, within uncertainties. This indicates that SF in low-mass SB galaxies is uniformly enhanced throughout the galaxy, regardless of the mechanism that triggers the SB. This contrasts with observations in massive galaxies, where SF is centrally concentrated in merger-driven SB systems. The lack of central concentration of SF in low-mass merger systems could be due to their shallow gravitational potentials and the compression of extended gaseous envelopes during interactions, which trigger SF across these galaxies. Deeper, higher-spatial-resolution observations are essential for better understanding the spatial distribution of SF in low-mass galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using GALEX FUV imaging of 272 isolated dwarf starbursts (17 post-merger, 255 non-interacting), the authors find star formation rate surface density is enhanced roughly uniformly across all radial bins in both subsamples, unlike massive merger-driven starbursts where star formation is centrally concentrated.
AI.motivation: In high-mass (M* > 10^10 Msun) starbursts, merger-driven systems show centrally concentrated star formation while secularly driven ones show uniform enhancement. Whether this spatial dichotomy extends to low-mass (M* < 10^10 Msun) starburst galaxies is unknown.
AI.method: Sample of 272 isolated starburst dwarf galaxies (17 post-merger, 255 non-interacting) in a 1 Mpc^3 volume, with stellar masses 10^7-10^9.6 Msun and z = 0.01-0.12. GALEX FUV imaging is used to derive star formation rates; the spatial variation of starburst activity is assessed by comparing SFR surface density (SFRD) in radial bins between the post-merger and non-interacting subsamples.
AI.result: SFRD is enhanced across all radial bins in both subsamples, and the enhancement is approximately uniform across the galaxies within uncertainties. No central concentration is detected in the post-merger dwarfs.
AI.conclusion: Star formation in low-mass starburst galaxies is uniformly enhanced regardless of the triggering mechanism, contrasting with massive merger-driven systems. The absence of central concentration in low-mass mergers may arise from shallow gravitational potentials and compression of extended gaseous envelopes during interactions. Deeper, higher-spatial-resolution observations are needed to confirm the spatial distribution of star formation in low-mass galaxies.

title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows
summary: Molecular clouds exhibit complex, multi-scale dynamics driven by the interplay of turbulence, self-gravity, and gas pressure. Modelling these systems with conventional grid-based methods becomes increasingly expensive as spatial resolution and dimensionality increase. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative by incorporating the governing equations directly into the training objective, but their ability to model realistic turbulent self-gravitating flows remains largely unexplored. We apply PINNs to isothermal molecular clouds initialized with astrophysically motivated turbulent velocity fields, considering subsonic and supersonic evolution in two and three dimensions. We benchmark the predicted density and velocity fields against the finite-volume code Athena++. PINNs accurately recover the global evolution of the flow over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, Mach numbers, and dimensionalities. Their training cost also exhibits weak dependence on spatial resolution, increasing by less than 25% from 128^3 to 1024^3 in our experiments. These results demonstrate that PINNs can model substantially more realistic self-gravitating turbulent flows than previously explored and provide a promising complementary framework for studying these systems.

AI.tldr: PINNs can model realistic self-gravitating turbulent molecular clouds across Mach numbers and dimensions, matching Athena++ global evolution while training cost scales weakly with resolution (<25% increase from 128^3 to 1024^3).
AI.motivation: Grid-based methods for molecular cloud dynamics become prohibitively expensive as resolution and dimensionality increase, and the feasibility of PINNs for realistic turbulent self-gravitating flows has been largely unexplored.
AI.method: Apply PINNs to isothermal molecular clouds initialized with astrophysically motivated turbulent velocity fields, for subsonic and supersonic cases in 2D and 3D, embedding the governing equations in the training objective; benchmark density and velocity fields against the finite-volume code Athena++.
AI.result: PINNs accurately recover global flow evolution over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, Mach numbers, and dimensionalities; training cost shows weak resolution dependence, increasing <25% from 128^3 to 1024^3.
AI.conclusion: PINNs can model substantially more realistic self-gravitating turbulent flows than previously shown, offering a promising mesh-free complementary framework for studying molecular clouds.

title: Research of signs of star formation in three S0 galaxies - members of isolated pairs
comment: 23 pages, 15 figures, 8 tables. Accepted in Res. Astron. Astrophys
summary: We obtained and analyzed long-slit spectra of three lenticular galaxies with optical rings: PGC 48114, ESO 234-011, and ESO 444-076. Ionized gas was detected in all of them. In PGC 48114, the excitation mechanism of the ionized gas differs along the ring, despite the consistent kinematics of the ionized gas and stars, as we showed earlier. Narrow-band images of PGC 48114 in the H$α$ and [NII]$λ$6583 emission lines revealed a star formation arc in the northwestern part of the ring. In ESO 234-011 and ESO 444-076, the ionized gas along the long slit is shock-excited and have kinematic discrepancy with the stars. This implies accretion of matter at an angle to the main disk of the S0 galaxies, which likely inhibits ongoing star formation. The companions of these S0 galaxies are late-type galaxies with extensive ongoing star formation. These companions may be the sources of the gas, or each pair may be feeding from a common gas reservoir.

AI.tldr: Long-slit spectroscopy of three ringed lenticular galaxies (PGC 48114, ESO 234-011, ESO 444-076) reveals ionized gas in all; only PGC 48114 shows a star-forming arc, while the other two show shock-excited gas with kinematic misalignment relative to the stars, pointing to external gas accretion.
AI.motivation: To understand the origin and excitation of ionized gas in S0 galaxies with optical rings, and whether gas accretion (possibly from companions) sustains or suppresses star formation in these systems.
AI.method: Long-slit spectroscopy of the three galaxies; analysis of ionized-gas excitation mechanisms and comparison of gas versus stellar kinematics; supplemented by narrow-band Hα and [NII]λ6583 imaging of PGC 48114 to map star formation.
AI.result: Ionized gas detected in all three galaxies. In PGC 48114 the excitation mechanism varies along the ring despite consistent gas–stellar kinematics, and narrow-band imaging reveals a star-forming arc in the NW part of the ring. In ESO 234-011 and ESO 444-076 the gas along the slit is shock-excited and kinematically decoupled from the stars. Both latter galaxies have late-type, actively star-forming companions.
AI.conclusion: The kinematic decoupling and shock excitation in ESO 234-011 and ESO 444-076 imply gas accretion at an angle to the main S0 disk, which likely inhibits ongoing star formation. The late-type companions may be the gas donors or both members may feed from a common gas reservoir.

title: One-Million-Year-Old Nascent Eclipsing Binaries in the LMC
summary: The light curves of nascent eclipsing binaries (EBs) feature sinusoidal reflection effects as a hot B-type main-sequence (MS) primary irradiates the near side of a cool, low-mass, pre-MS companion. We obtained multi-epoch echelle spectra with the MIKE spectrograph on the 6.5m Magellan-Clay Telescope of three nascent EBs embedded in H II regions within the LMC. By fitting atmospheric models to the spectra, the primaries are found to be mid-B dwarfs (T_eff,1 = 18,600-22,800 K; M_1 = 6.8-8.5 Msun). The dynamical masses of the secondaries are only M_2 = 0.38-0.95 Msun, yielding extremely small mass ratios q = M_2/M_1 = 0.05-0.11. Unlike solar-type primaries, which exhibit a dearth of close companions with q < 0.1 known as the brown dwarf desert, massive stars can readily form with very close companions below q < 0.1. By fitting PHOEBE models to the OGLE-III light curves, we measure the secondary radii R_2 = 2.0-2.8 Rsun and temperatures T_eff,2 = 4,000 K. The pre-MS companions are located high on the Hayashi track where evolutionary models indicate ages of only 1 Myr. Their extreme youth suggests that nascent EBs formed via inward disk migration during the previous embedded protostellar phase.

AI.tldr: Multiple-epoch MIKE spectra of three nascent eclipsing binaries in LMC H II regions reveal mid-B dwarf primaries irradiated by extremely low-mass pre-MS companions, giving mass ratios q = 0.05-0.11.
AI.motivation: The brown dwarf desert describes the dearth of close companions with q < 0.1 to solar-type primaries; whether massive primaries exhibit similar suppression of low-mass companions, and how nascent binaries in this regime form and evolve, is unclear.
AI.method: Multi-epoch echelle spectroscopy with the MIKE spectrograph on Magellan-Clay (6.5 m) of three nascent eclipsing binaries embedded in LMC H II regions; atmospheric model fitting for primary parameters; dynamical masses for secondaries; PHOEBE fits to OGLE-III light curves for radii and temperatures; comparison with pre-MS evolutionary models (Hayashi track).
AI.result: Primaries are mid-B dwarfs (T_eff,1 = 18,600-22,800 K; M_1 = 6.8-8.5 Msun). Secondary dynamical masses are M_2 = 0.38-0.95 Msun, giving q = 0.05-0.11. Light-curve fitting yields R_2 = 2.0-2.8 Rsun and T_eff,2 about 4,000 K. The secondaries lie high on the Hayashi track, with evolutionary ages of only about 1 Myr.
AI.conclusion: Unlike solar-type primaries, massive stars can readily form with very close companions below q < 0.1. The extreme youth of the pre-MS companions suggests these nascent eclipsing binaries formed via inward disk migration during the preceding embedded protostellar phase.

title: The Physics of the Cold and Warm Interstellar Medium Through Radio Recombination Lines
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Salas01
summary: The interplay between star formation and the interstellar medium (ISM) gives rise to a feedback cycle that is one of the key drivers of galaxy evolution. The coldest gas in the ISM provides the fuel for star formation, and, in turn, the ISM is affected by feedback in the form of photons, shocks, and cosmic rays. Radio recombination lines (RRLs) offer a unique way of characterizing the gas in the ISM as extinction free probes of the gas kinematics, density, temperature, and radiation field. Hydrogen RRLs (HRRLs) probe gas where hydrogen is ionized, while carbon RRLs (CRRLs) probe cold gas in the HI-to-H$_{2}$ transition layers. The superb sensitivity, spatial resolution, large field of view, and frequency resolution and coverage of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will allow for efficient observations of RRLs, that will make significant impacts to the study of the diffuse ISM. By observing RRLs with the SKA we will be able to determine the thermal and turbulent balance, chemical enrichment, sizes, and ionization rate of the cold and ionized gases from degree-scales down to arcsecond scales in our Galaxy.

AI.tldr: Radio recombination lines (RRLs) are extinction-free probes of the interstellar medium (ISM), and the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will enable efficient, high-sensitivity RRL observations that significantly advance studies of the diffuse ISM.
AI.motivation: The feedback cycle between star formation and the ISM drives galaxy evolution; the coldest ISM gas fuels star formation while being affected by feedback (photons, shocks, cosmic rays). Characterizing this gas requires extinction-free tracers of kinematics, density, temperature, and radiation field, which RRLs uniquely provide.
AI.method: Use hydrogen RRLs (HRRLs) to probe ionized gas and carbon RRLs (CRRLs) to probe cold gas in HI-to-H2 transition layers, exploiting the SKA's sensitivity, spatial resolution, wide field of view, and frequency resolution/coverage for efficient RRL surveys.
AI.result: SKA RRL observations will enable determination of the thermal and turbulent balance, chemical enrichment, physical sizes, and ionization rate of cold and ionized gas across spatial scales from degree-scale down to arcsecond-scale within our Galaxy.
AI.conclusion: RRL observations with the SKA constitute a powerful, extinction-free approach to characterizing the diffuse ISM and will make significant contributions to understanding the star formation–ISM feedback cycle and galaxy evolution.

title: Complete Multi-Band Structural Characterization for 10 Million Galaxies in the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey using Deep Learning
summary: Galaxy structure is wavelength-dependent, as different photometric bands trace distinct stellar populations and structural components. We present per-galaxy Bayesian posterior distributions of the bulge-to-total light ratio ($L_B/L_T$), effective radius ($R_e$), and flux ($F$) in the $g$, $r$, and $i$ bands for nearly $10$ million galaxies across $\sim$1400\,deg$^2$ of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP) Wide survey at $z \leq 0.75$ and $m < 23$. To our knowledge, this is the largest multi-band catalog of bulge--disk structural parameters with per-galaxy posteriors. $\sim$3.9 million of the above galaxies have full multi-band coverage. Measurements are generated using the Galaxy Morphology Posterior Estimation Network (\gampen{}), a Bayesian deep-learning framework. We demonstrate that we can adapt \gampen{} from previously-trained single-band models to the new bands by using transfer learning on only $\sim$0.5\% of our dataset. Despite this extremely small training set, \gampen{} successfully reproduces light-profile fitting measurements and its output posteriors are extremely well-calibrated with $\lesssim6\%$ mean deviation. This approach offers a scalable pathway to structural parameter measurements with robust uncertainties for Rubin, Euclid, and Roman data, which we will pursue in forthcoming work. While structural measurements remain robust across most bands and redshift ranges, performance degrades significantly for the $g$-band at $z \gtrsim 0.5$, where it increasingly probes rest-frame ultraviolet emission; these measurements are therefore excluded from the public release. This public catalog will enable large-scale statistical studies of morphological color gradients, wavelength-dependent galaxy structure, and galaxy evolution.
