AI.tldr: The authors release the largest multi-band catalog of bulge-disk structural parameters with per-galaxy Bayesian posteriors (~10 million galaxies in g, r, i bands from HSC-SSP), generated with the GAMPEN deep-learning framework and adapted to new bands via transfer learning on only ~0.5% of the data.
AI.motivation: Galaxy structure is wavelength-dependent because different photometric bands trace distinct stellar populations and structural components, motivating large-scale, multi-band structural measurements with reliable uncertainties.
AI.method: Bayesian deep-learning framework GAMPEN is used to infer bulge-to-total light ratio, effective radius, and flux per galaxy in g, r, and i bands. Single-band pre-trained models are adapted to new bands via transfer learning on ~0.5% of the dataset. Applied to ~10 million galaxies over ~1400 deg^2 of HSC-SSP Wide at z<=0.75 and m<23.
AI.result: GAMPEN reproduces light-profile fitting measurements and yields extremely well-calibrated posteriors with mean deviation <~6%. About 3.9 million galaxies have full multi-band coverage. Structural measurements are robust across most bands and redshifts, but degrade significantly for g-band at z>~0.5 (rest-frame UV), so these are excluded from the public release.
AI.conclusion: The public catalog enables large-scale statistical studies of morphological color gradients, wavelength-dependent structure, and galaxy evolution. The transfer-learning approach offers a scalable pathway to structural measurements with robust uncertainties for Rubin, Euclid, and Roman data.

title: A Population Synthesis Model for Odd Radio Circles Produced by Shock-Bubble Interactions
summary: Odd Radio Circles (ORCs) are edge-brightened rings of diffuse radio emission of roughly arcminute size whose physical origin remains debated. One proposed mechanism is vortex formation through Shock-Bubble interaction (SBI), in which a merger or accretion shock re-energizes a fossil radio lobe into an edge-brightened ring. We test whether this mechanism can reproduce the observed ORC abundance using a Monte Carlo population-synthesis model that combines the galaxy stellar mass function, the radio-AGN incidence relation, dark-matter halo merger histories, and the inflation and buoyant survival of AGN-inflated bubbles, with synthetic radio fluxes and ring geometries drawn from a grid of magnetohydrodynamic SBI simulations. Applying survey-specific selection to the ASKAP-EMU Pilot Survey (944 MHz) and the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS; 144 MHz), we predict $2.7^{+3.9}_{-1.6}$ detectable ORCs in the EMU Pilot, matching the three found there, and $268^{+331}_{-148}$ in LoTSS, of which $7.5^{+9.5}_{-4.2}$ have a counterpart at 1.4 GHz. The predicted hosts are mostly central galaxies in group-scale halos. The predicted rings are physically smaller and lie at lower redshifts than the galaxies identified as hosts of the known ORCs, suggesting that SBI produces mainly the nearby part of the ORC population, or that some ORCs are associated with the wrong host. The population synthesis model also predicts a large population of low surface brightness steep-spectrum ORCs in the LoTSS band, implying a large hidden population and predicting that deeper low-frequency surveys should uncover many more ORCs than are currently known. These results indicate that shock-bubble interactions can account for at least part of the observed incidence of ORCs.

AI.tldr: A Monte Carlo population-synthesis model shows that shock-bubble interaction (SBI) can reproduce the observed abundance of Odd Radio Circles in the ASKAP-EMU Pilot and predicts a large hidden steep-spectrum ORC population in LoTSS.
AI.motivation: ORCs are arcminute-scale edge-brightened diffuse radio rings of uncertain physical origin. One proposed mechanism is vortex formation via shock-bubble interaction, in which a merger or accretion shock re-energizes a fossil radio lobe into an edge-brightened ring. The paper tests whether SBI can reproduce the observed ORC abundance.
AI.method: Monte Carlo population synthesis combining the galaxy stellar mass function, the radio-AGN incidence relation, dark-matter halo merger histories, and AGN-inflated bubble inflation and buoyant survival, with synthetic radio fluxes and ring geometries drawn from a grid of MHD SBI simulations. Survey-specific selection is applied to the ASKAP-EMU Pilot (944 MHz) and LoTSS (144 MHz).
AI.result: Predicts 2.7^{+3.9}_{-1.6} detectable ORCs in EMU Pilot (matching the 3 observed) and 268^{+331}_{-148} in LoTSS, of which 7.5^{+9.5}_{-4.2} have a 1.4 GHz counterpart. Predicted hosts are mostly central galaxies in group-scale halos. Predicted rings are smaller and at lower redshift than hosts of known ORCs, suggesting SBI produces mainly the nearby ORC population or that some ORCs are misassigned hosts. A large population of low-surface-brightness steep-spectrum ORCs is predicted in the LoTSS band.
AI.conclusion: SBI can account for at least part of the observed ORC incidence, and a large hidden ORC population should be uncovered by deeper low-frequency surveys.

title: A probabilistic approach to separate mergers and jellyfish galaxies: Application of morphological non-parametric indexes to the DESI Legacy Survey
comment: Submitted to A&A. 18 pages, 15 figures, 6 tables
summary: Galaxy morphology traces the physical processes that shape galaxy evolution, but non-parametric diagnostic boundaries depend on image quality and preprocessing. We investigate the classification of regular spirals, regular ellipticals, mergers, and jellyfish (ram-pressure-stripping candidate) galaxies in the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. Using galmex measurements of ten non-parametric morphological indices, we evaluate two-dimensional diagnostic planes with a cross-validated Bayesian kernel-density classifier and combine all indices using probability-calibrated LightGBM models. For separating regular spirals, regular ellipticals, and perturbed systems, the most informative planes combine Shannon entropy with $M_{20}$ or asymmetry indices, reaching balanced accuracies of 0.76-0.77. We provide survey-specific probabilistic boundaries in the entropy-$M_{20}$ and entropy-shape-asymmetry planes. Separating mergers from jellyfish candidates is more challenging; the best two-dimensional combinations, all involving concentration, reach balanced accuracies of approximately 0.73. The calibrated three-class LightGBM model achieves a balanced accuracy and macro-F1 score of 0.89, while the four-class model achieves 0.75 and 0.76, respectively. We provide class probabilities and preferred classifications for 1,744,454 galaxies. Our results show that non-parametric morphology identifies broad structural disturbance reliably, but distinguishing its physical origin is harder: jellyfish candidates occupy a relatively coherent region of parameter space, whereas mergers span diverse and overlapping morphologies.

AI.tldr: Non-parametric morphology with calibrated Bayesian KDE planes and LightGBM reliably separates regular spirals, ellipticals, and disturbed galaxies (BA≈0.89) but struggles to distinguish mergers from jellyfish candidates (BA≈0.75).
AI.motivation: Non-parametric diagnostic boundaries for galaxy morphology are sensitive to image quality and preprocessing, so survey-specific, probability-calibrated classification of regular spirals, regular ellipticals, mergers, and jellyfish (ram-pressure-stripping) candidates in DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys is needed.
AI.method: Uses galmex measurements of ten non-parametric morphological indices on DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys galaxies; evaluates 2D diagnostic planes with a cross-validated Bayesian kernel-density classifier, and combines all indices via probability-calibrated LightGBM models (three- and four-class).
AI.result: Most informative planes combine Shannon entropy with M20 or asymmetry, reaching balanced accuracies 0.76–0.77; survey-specific probabilistic boundaries provided in entropy–M20 and entropy–shape-asymmetry planes. Merger vs. jellyfish separation is hardest (best 2D combos all involve concentration, BA≈0.73). Calibrated three-class LightGBM: BA and macro-F1 = 0.89; four-class: 0.75 and 0.76. Class probabilities and preferred classifications released for 1,744,454 galaxies.
AI.conclusion: Non-parametric morphology reliably identifies broad structural disturbance, but disentangling its physical origin is harder: jellyfish candidates occupy a coherent region of parameter space while mergers span diverse, overlapping morphologies.
